newsitem.title: USA: Health of U.S.-jailed Egyptian cleric worsens - lawyers.
newsitem.headline: Health of U.S.-jailed Egyptian cleric worsens - lawyers.

text.p: The health of the Moslem cleric who was convicted for conspiracy to bomb New York landmarks and assassinate political leaders has so deteriorated in jail that his life could be in danger, his lawyers said on Friday.

The lawyers, including former U.S. Attorney General Ramsay Clark, said that regulations imposed by the U.S. government were to blame for Egyptian Sheikh Omar Abdel-Rahman's failing health. The sheikh is blind and has long suffered from diabetes, asthma and a heart condition.

U.S. prison authorities said the cleric was being treated fairly under the regulations introduced in May 1996 for prisoners linked with terrorism. The rules restrict contact with his wife to once a month and he can place calls only to his lawyers.

"It sounds like the sheikh's condition is deteriorating and obviously could be life-threatening. He is having trouble breathing, suffering severe headaches, itching from allergies and has abdominal pain around his liver and kidneys," Clark told Reuters.
Lynne Stewart, the lawyer who reperesented Abdel-Rahman in his 1995 trial, said: "They have given him a slow death sentence."
Clark said that for more than a month Abdel-Rahman had been kept in virtual isolation in a damp basement cell at Springfield federal prison in Missouri. Clark said the cell had no ventiliation.
"We would dispute any claim that he is not being treated humanely and fairly," U.S. Bureau of Prisons spokesman Dan Dunne said.

In a May 1 letter to the Springfield prison warden, Pat Keohane, Clark complains that "the conditions of the air in his cell have worsened. He now puts water on the floor before sleeping, and sleeps on the floor with his face covered by a wet cloth in order to breath more easily."

Clark, who also represented the blind cleric at his trial and is handling his appeal, said Abdel-Rahman had not been given tapes containing readings from the Koran and other religious texts he sent him.

Abdel-Rahman and nine others were convicted in October 1995 of conspiracy to carry out a war of terrorism that included blowing up the United Nations, other New York City landmarks and plans to assassinate political leaders including Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak.
